questions.stem: How many addresses does a formal letter carry?

options.text: Two — the writer's address and the recipient's address
Three — the writer's, the recipient's and the postal agent's
None; addresses are written on the envelope only

questions.explanation: A formal letter is an official document that may be filed, so it must show both parties. The writer's address establishes where a reply should be sent, and the recipient's address, written below it on the left, records who was officially addressed. An informal letter carries only the writer's address.

distractorRationale.a: This is the informal letter format, and using it for an official letter costs format marks
distractorRationale.c: No such third address exists in any letter format
distractorRationale.d: The envelope is not marked; the letter itself must carry the addresses

questions.stem: A letter begins with the salutation "Dear Sir". Which subscription must close it?
questions.explanation: When you do not name the recipient — *Dear Sir*, *Dear Madam*, *Dear Sir or Madam* — the letter closes with *Yours faithfully*. The pairing is fixed, and a mismatch is one of the easiest format marks to lose.

distractorRationale.a: *Yours sincerely* goes with a named recipient, as in *Dear Mr Okafor*
distractorRationale.c: *Yours affectionately* belongs to letters to close family and friends
distractorRationale.d: *Yours truly* is an American convention and is not expected in these examinations

questions.stem: A letter of application begins "Dear Mr Okafor". Which subscription is correct?
questions.explanation: Because the recipient is named, the correct close is *Yours sincerely*. Note the spelling and capitalisation: *Yours* takes a capital Y and no apostrophe, while *sincerely* stays in lower case.

distractorRationale.a: *Yours faithfully* is reserved for unnamed recipients such as *Dear Sir*
distractorRationale.c: *Your* is the possessive determiner; the fixed form of the subscription is *Yours*
distractorRationale.d: *Yours obediently* is archaic and no longer used in modern official correspondence

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the correct order of the features of a formal letter?

options.text: Writer's address, date, recipient's address, salutation, heading, body, subscription, signature and name
Salutation, writer's address, date, heading, body, recipient's address, signature
Writer's address, salutation, recipient's address, date, body, heading, signature
Date, heading, salutation, writer's address, body, subscription, recipient's address

questions.explanation: The order moves from the writer outward: your own address, the date, then the address of the person you are writing to, then the greeting, the subject heading, the message itself, the close and finally your signature above your full name in block letters.

distractorRationale.b: Puts the salutation before the addresses and buries the recipient's address at the end
distractorRationale.c: Separates the date from the writer's address and places the heading after the body
distractorRationale.d: Opens with the heading before any greeting and ends with the recipient's address

questions.stem: Which sentence is best suited to a formal letter of complaint to a bank manager?

options.text: I'm writing 'cos your ATM swallowed my card last week and nobody has done anything.
I wish to report that your automated teller machine retained my card on 4 August and that the matter is still unresolved.
Your ATM chopped my card and your staff just kept looking at me anyhow.
Please o, my card is still inside your machine since last week.

questions.explanation: Formal register calls for complete words rather than contractions, precise dates rather than vague time references, and neutral vocabulary rather than emotive or colloquial expressions. Option b gives the manager the exact information needed to act on the complaint.

distractorRationale.a: Uses the contraction *I'm* and the colloquial *'cos*, and gives only a vague date
distractorRationale.c: *Chopped* and *anyhow* belong to informal Nigerian speech, not to official writing
distractorRationale.d: The particle *o* and the pleading tone are features of casual conversation

questions.stem: Where does the heading, or subject of the letter, belong in a formal letter?

options.text: Above the writer's address, at the very top of the page
Immediately after the salutation and before the first paragraph of the body
At the end, just above the signature
A formal letter never carries a heading

questions.explanation: The heading sits between the salutation and the body, and it is usually underlined or written in capital letters — for example APPLICATION FOR THE POST OF LABORATORY ASSISTANT. Its purpose is to tell a busy official the subject of the letter before reading a word of the message.

distractorRationale.a: Nothing goes above the writer's address
distractorRationale.c: A heading placed at the end serves no purpose, since the reader has already finished
distractorRationale.d: A heading is one of the features that distinguishes formal from informal letters

questions.stem: Contractions such as *don't*, *can't* and *I'm* are acceptable in a formal letter.
questions.explanation: False. Formal writing uses full forms: *do not*, *cannot*, *I am*. Contractions belong to speech and to informal letters, and a formal letter peppered with them loses register marks even when every sentence is grammatical.

questions.stem: You are writing to the Chairman of your Local Government about a collapsed bridge. Which closing paragraph is most appropriate?

options.text: That is all I have to say. Thank you.
I therefore appeal to you to direct the works department to repair the bridge before the peak of the rains, and I look forward to your favourable response.
If nothing is done about this bridge, we shall know that you do not care about us at all.
Please try and do something about the bridge as soon as you can, my brother.

questions.explanation: A formal closing paragraph should restate the specific action requested, give a reason for urgency, and end courteously. Option b does all three while keeping a respectful, businesslike tone.

distractorRationale.a: Abrupt and vague; it requests no action and gives the reader nothing to act on
distractorRationale.c: Threatening in tone, which is inappropriate in official correspondence and weakens the appeal
distractorRationale.d: *My brother* treats an official as a personal acquaintance, breaking the formal register

questions.stem: Which heading is best for a letter applying to teach chemistry at a secondary school?

options.text: APPLICATION FOR THE POST OF CHEMISTRY TEACHER
I WANT A JOB IN YOUR SCHOOL PLEASE

questions.explanation: A heading should name the purpose of the letter precisely and impersonally, so that the recipient can route it correctly without reading the body. Option b states both the action — an application — and the exact post being sought.

distractorRationale.a: Says nothing about the subject of the letter
distractorRationale.c: Written as a personal plea rather than a subject line, and includes a courtesy word that does not belong in a heading
distractorRationale.d: A single word that names a school subject, not the purpose of the letter

questions.stem: A candidate's formal letter to a Commissioner for Education opens "Dear Sir" and closes "Yours sincerely, Tunde". Identify the two faults.

options.text: The salutation should be *Dear Madam*, and the name should be in italics
The subscription should be *Yours faithfully*, and the writer's full name should be given in block letters below the signature
The salutation should be *Dear Commissioner*, and the subscription should be *Yours truly*
There is no fault; both the salutation and the subscription are correct

questions.explanation: *Dear Sir* does not name the recipient, so the fixed partner is *Yours faithfully*, not *Yours sincerely*. In addition, a formal letter identifies its author fully: the signature is followed by the writer's full name, usually in block letters, so that the reader knows exactly who wrote.

distractorRationale.a: The gender of the salutation is not in question, and italics play no part in letter conventions
distractorRationale.c: *Dear Commissioner* is not a standard salutation, and *Yours truly* is not used in these examinations
distractorRationale.d: There are two clear format faults

questions.stem: What is the purpose of including two addresses in a formal letter?

options.text: To provide a return address and the recipient's address
To make the letter look longer

questions.explanation: The two addresses in a formal letter serve important purposes. The sender's address allows the recipient to respond, while the recipient's address ensures the letter reaches the correct person or organization.

distractorRationale.b: This option is incorrect because formal letters should be concise and to the point.
distractorRationale.c: Confusing the reader is not a goal of formal writing.
distractorRationale.d: Unnecessary information is discouraged in formal letters.
